item.title: New York City gunman appeared to target NFL, had mental health history
item.description:
The Manhattan high-rise shooter, a former high school football player, left a note referencing the brain disease CTE and appeared to have targeted the NFL’s offices, authorities said.

The man who opened fire in a Manhattan office building Monday carried a letter in which he speculated that he suffered from traumatic brain injury and blamed the National Football League for his struggles, authorities said Tuesday.

Police said Shane Tamura, a 27-year-old former high school football player, had a “documented mental health history” and appeared to be targeting the NFL when he opened fire, killing four people and injuring a fifth before turning the gun on himself.

In his handwritten letter, which law enforcement found in his wallet, the gunman said he believed he suffered from chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE — a degenerative brain disease that can be diagnosed only posthumously — and pleaded, “Study my brain please.”

On the third page of the letter, Tamura apologized and said the NFL “knowingly concealed the dangers to our brains to maximize profits. They failed us,” according to a law enforcement official who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly.

Tamura never played in the NFL and does not appear to have played football beyond high school.

Authorities said he appears to have driven through the weekend from his home in Las Vegas to reach the 44-story building at 345 Park Ave. where he opened fire. While investigators are still working to confirm the shooter’s motive, New York Mayor Eric Adams said authorities “have reason to believe he was focused on the NFL,” which is headquartered in the building. Adams said investigators believe the shooter was trying to reach the NFL’s suite of offices but took the wrong elevator.

CTE is a degenerative brain disease caused by repeated head injuries, including those suffered by football players and athletes in other violent sports, and has been linked to memory loss, depression and other symptoms. High-profile suicides and violent outbursts by former NFL players have forced a years-long reckoning by the league, its fans and former players, thousands of whom sued the NFL for its role in their injuries. Most of the high-profile CTE cases involve athletes who played football for several years, though researchers have discovered CTE cases in younger people with far less exposure to the bruising game.

“The motive appeared to be connected to the shooter’s belief that he was suffering from CTE, he was an ex-NFL player,” Adams said during a CNN appearance Tuesday. “Those items just don’t pan out — he never played for NFL — and so we’re still unraveling this terrible shooting that took place in the city.”

Tamura lived in Las Vegas, where police say he worked overnight security at the Horseshoe Las Vegas casino. He failed to show up for his scheduled shift Sunday, and New York police dispatched investigators to Las Vegas on Tuesday.

Tamura’s neighborhood in a gated community west of the city was quiet early Tuesday evening as temperatures hovered above 100 degrees. A few locals walked their dogs on the sidewalks, and a postal worker delivered mail. Police officers who stood guard at the marble entrance Tuesday had moved on, but several neighbors still drove slowly through the exits and gawked at the local news trucks lining the boulevard outside.

According to the Los Angeles Times, Tamura is the son of a former police officer; Terence Tamura spent many years stationed in the San Fernando Valley for the Los Angeles Police Department.

Tamura attended high schools in Southern California, where he played football for Golden Valley High School in Santa Clarita, according to the Santa Clarita Valley Signal and a 2014 Ventura County Star report. The Signal reported that its football preview from October 2014 described him as a standout running back who came “out of nowhere to become one of the most electrifying players in the league” and that he had been featured in the junior varsity preview the year before.

He then played his senior season with Granada Hills Charter, where he was a standout running back and defensive back and also returned kicks.

Jason Rosser, 26, said he and other former teammates from Granada Hills were struggling to process Monday’s events, saying Tamura’s actions don’t line up with their memories of the low-key teenager with whom they once shared a locker room.

“He was a really laid-back, quiet guy,” Rosser said. “Just really shocking. It’s hard to put words behind it. He was just so quiet and so friendly. It doesn’t make sense.”

Another teammate recalled that by the time Tamura showed up to Granada Hills football practice in late summer 2015, the other players already had been given their equipment. Tamura was issued an older model of helmet, which the players jokingly called “concussion buckets” because they didn’t absorb contact as well, said Marc Schmitz, a former teammate.

Schmitz recalled Tamura as a fearless ballcarrier, despite being listed at just 5-foot-7 and 140 pounds.

“He just had this motor. He wasn’t a big guy by any means,” Schmitz said. “He was definitely a smaller running back. He ran hard. He didn’t shy away from hitting, but he was a speed back, an elusive-type guy. He made people miss.”

Schmitz and Rosser said they had not spoken with Tamura in recent years, and neither could recall any injuries that Tamura might have suffered during his time with Granada Hills.

In the hours after the shooting, a YouTube video with Tamura resurfaced online. It features a high-school-age Tamura after a game in which he scored two touchdowns in a come-from-behind win.

“We were down 10-0; we definitely had to stay disciplined,” Tamura said, smiling and rocking from side to side. “Our coach kept saying, ‘Don’t hold your heads down, don’t hold your heads down.’ We just had to stay disciplined and come together as a team.”

New York City Police Commissioner Jessica S. Tisch said at a news conference late Monday that, just before 6:30 p.m., Tamura double-parked a black BMW on Park Avenue and entered the high-rise through its main entrance while holding an AR-style rifle.

He killed four people in the building: off-duty New York police officer Didarul Islam, security guard Aland Etienne, Blackstone employee Wesley LePatner, and Julia Hyman, an associate with the company that managed the building.

One man was in critical but stable condition at New York-Presbyterian Hospital on Monday night, Tisch said. The injured man is NFL employee Craig Clementi, who works in the league’s finance department, said a person with knowledge of the situation who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly. All other NFL employees were safe and accounted for, according to an email NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell sent to league employees.

According to Tisch, the shooter had a gun license from Nevada and a “documented mental health history.” Police searching his vehicle after the shooting found a rifle case with a loaded revolver, ammunition, a backpack and medication that had been prescribed to him.

He appears to have driven across the country over the weekend, traveling through Colorado on Saturday and then Nebraska and Iowa on Sunday, Tisch said. An initial investigation showed he was in Columbia, New Jersey, at 4:24 p.m. before heading into New York City shortly afterward.

While CTE is often associated with prolonged professional football careers and years of repeated exposure to head trauma, the degenerative brain disease has been diagnosed in young athletes whose football careers never advanced beyond the high school field.

Ann McKee, the director of Boston University’s CTE Center, said she would not be surprised to discover that Tamura had been suffering from the effects of CTE.

“I do think it’s possible he has CTE because we have seen it in former high school players with just that amount of exposure,” McKee said in an interview. “Of course, it’s more common in individuals who play longer periods of football, but it is possible. It’s also possible he has a mental health disorder.”

McKee is among the world’s leading CTE researchers and co-wrote a 2023 study that found 41 percent of a sample of former athletes who were 30 or younger at the time of death had evidence of CTE. Eighty-four percent of brain donors in the study were amateur athletes. McKee noted that there was selection bias associated with the study and that the numbers probably do not reflect the general population of athletes. But the study did show that young athletes are susceptible to the disease and that the pathology of CTE can start early.

McKee is also the neuropathologist credited with some of the highest-profile CTE diagnoses, including of former athletes who were prone to violence, such as Aaron Hernandez, the former NFL tight end who was serving a life sentence for murder when he killed himself in 2017, and Phillip Adams, a 32-year-old former NFL player who killed six people and himself in 2021.

“There is some precedent linking individuals with known CTE and rampages of violence,” McKee said. “We’ve seen it in young players, former football players.”

She explained that damage to the frontal lobe caused by repeated blows to the head could result in impulsivity, poor judgment or violent outbursts. It is not known what types of injuries Tamura might have suffered during his high school playing career.

McKee was not certain of the fate of Tamura’s brain and whether it would end up in her brain bank for study. Adams told CNN on Tuesday that the city’s chief medical examiner will decide whether to test for CTE.

Roman Stubbs in Las Vegas and Mark Maske contributed to this report.

item.title: Shooting victims include ‘hero’ security guard, executive, immigrant NYPD officer
item.description:
Four people were killed and another person was seriously wounded Monday evening when a gunman opened fire inside a Midtown Manhattan high-rise.

NEW YORK — They were a cross section of New York City: A Haitian security guard standing watch in a Midtown lobby. A Jewish executive involved in the city’s philanthropic circles, and a young woman just beginning her career. A Bangladeshi police officer — a father expecting his third child — serving the place he now called home.

Their lives, varied and vibrant as the nation’s largest city, ended Monday night when a man with an assault rifle shot his way inside a 44-story skyscraper large enough to have its own Zip code. Police said the shooter killed four people, critically wounded another and then turned the gun on himself.

On Tuesday, as details of the shooting at 345 Park Ave. and identities of the victims emerged, communities across the city expressed sorrow for the lost and wounded.

Here are their stories.

Didarul Islam, 36

A native of Bangladesh, Didarul Islam immigrated to the United States before joining the NYPD as an officer 3½ years ago, the department said. Islam was assigned to the 47th Precinct in the Bronx but was moonlighting as uniformed private security at 345 Park Ave. on Monday night. He was married with two young sons, New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch told reporters Monday, adding that Islam’s wife is pregnant with the couple’s third child.

“He was doing the job that we asked him to do,” Tisch said. “He put himself in harm’s way. He made the ultimate sacrifice, shot in cold blood, wearing a uniform that stood for the promise that he made to this city. He died as he lived: a hero.”

As an NYPD helicopter flew overhead Tuesday afternoon, officers on motorcycles led a procession of Islam’s body from the medical examiner’s office to Parkchester Jame Masjid, a mosque in his Parkchester neighborhood of the Bronx. Islam’s family sobbed as his remains were transferred.

Islam had worked as a school safety officer before joining the NYPD, NYC Police Benevolent Association President Patrick Hendry told reporters outside the mosque. He said it was unclear whether Islam was able to return fire Monday before the gunman killed him.

“He was about providing for his family, working every day, no matter what it took,” Hendry said. “He was the sole provider of his family, and that’s what he did every day.”

Islam’s father was hospitalized after the shooting, Hendry said. He declined to share the cause.

“This is a way our city can show his family that we will never forget this police officer, that he was willing to put his life on the line for the entire city,” Hendry said of the procession to the mosque. “And no one could have predicted that evil would have came to our city last night and preyed on innocent people.”

Zairul Islam, a relative of Didarul Islam, told The Washington Post that their family would be at the mosque Tuesday night to wash Didarul’s body and dress him in the white burial shroud known as “kaffan” to be interred.

Zairul said Didarul had called his wife from work before the shooting Monday and told her he would be home in three hours. He had been planning to go with her to a doctor’s appointment Tuesday.

Zairul described Didarul as hardworking and the type of person who “never says no.” He donated much of his salary to the mosques he attended and sent money to Bangladesh for families in need.

His parents and wife are devastated by his death, Zairul said.

“We cannot give them anything, you know, to make them calm,” Zairul said. “It’s very hard.”

In the Bronx, Islam’s death sent ripples through the borough’s tight-knit Bangladeshi community — a slice of New York where the officer was often spotted at restaurants on Sterling Avenue and walking to the Parkchester Islamic Center.

“I used to see him a lot on the street,” said 29-year-old Tanjim Talukder. “We used to walk to mosque together.”

The men would talk about politics in Bangladesh, Talukder said. “He was a friendly guy, humble. I feel so sad.”

Abdul Salaman echoed Talukder’s grief. Salaman knew Islam in Bangladesh, and the men stayed in touch as both eventually moved to the Bronx. “We grew up together,” Salaman said. “He was a very hardworking person.”

“They are very sad, everybody,” Salaman said after leaving the home where the officer lived with his wife and children. An NYPD vehicle sat watch outside.

At an elementary school across the street, a black gate stood decorated with blue and white roses, as well as a banner — emblazoned with a thin blue line American flag — calling Islam a “loving parent and NYPD hero.”

“Heroes in their quite grace/ Leave in our world, a brighter trace,” the poem on the banner read. “Their legacy, a path to follow/In their footsteps, we find tomorrow.”

Wesley LePatner, 43

A real estate investment executive with Blackstone since 2014, Wesley LePatner was remembered by friends and colleagues as kind, generous and well-respected in her field.

“It’s hard to put into words what a wonderful, beautiful, sweet, kind, and generous soul Wesley was. We will be there for the family, and we will never forget her,” Benny Rogosnitzky, a friend and congregant at LePatner’s synagogue, said in a Facebook post.

Blackstone in a statement said that LePatner was a wife and mother who embodied the best of the company, mourning her as a passionate and generous presence.

In addition to her work with Blackstone, LePatner served on multiple philanthropic boards, including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the United Jewish Appeal-Federation of New York, the Abraham Joshua Heschel School and the Yale University Library Council, according to her professional biography.

The UJA-Federation in a statement Tuesday said LePatner was “extraordinary in every way — personally, professionally, and philanthropically.”

Aland Etienne, 46

The security guard killed in Monday’s shooting in Manhattan was Aland Etienne, according to Manny Pastreich, president of 32BJ SEIU, one of New York’s largest unions representing workers including security guards, doormen and janitors.

Police said Etienne was shot while behind his security desk after a gunman burst into the lobby of the Midtown building.

Pastreich in a statement described Etienne as a dedicated employee “who took his job duties extremely seriously.” Etienne, Pastreich said, was “a New York hero.” “We will remember him as such.”

Etienne’s brother, Gathmand Etienne, wrote in a Facebook post that their family had been left “shattered” by his killing — and asked for prayers and strength as they navigate the unbearable.

“He was more than a brother — he was a father, a son, and a light in our lives,” Gathmand Etienne wrote.

“Rest in peace, Brother. You’ll never be forgotten,” he added.

Julia Hyman, 27

Julia Hyman, who graduated from Cornell University in 2020, was a warm, driven and passionate student, who left a “lasting impression” on those around her, school officials said. She had just visited the campus this summer for a five-year reunion with her classmates.

Hyman worked as an associate at Rudin Management, the company that managed 345 Park Ave. Hyman started her job in November, according to her LinkedIn page. In a statement Tuesday, the Rudin family described her as a “cherished” colleague.

Teachers and administrators at Riverdale Country School, a private school in the Bronx that Hyman graduated from in 2016, remembered her as having a “heart of gold” and a “desire to see others succeed,” the head of school said in a letter to community members.

“We are simply heartbroken by this loss, and will forever remember Julia for her light, her bright smile and infectious laugh, and the kindness and sense of community that she brought to school every day,” wrote Kari Ostrem, the head of school.

During her senior year, Hyman captained three varsity sports — soccer, swimming and lacrosse — and received an award that honors “that young woman who best demonstrated outstanding ability, leadership, and sportsmanship and the qualities of hard work, excellent attitude and responsibility to her teammates and school,” according to the letter.

Craig Clementi, age unknown

Craig Clementi, an NFL employee who works in the league’s finance department, was injured in Monday’s shooting, a person with knowledge of the situation said. His father-in-law, Robert Hunter, told the New York Daily News that Clementi “was on his way home when he got shot.”

He “came through the surgery and there was some spinal damage,” but he is “doing well,” Hunter said. Clementi is expected by doctors to recover from his injuries, according to a person familiar with the matter.

Bellware, Maske, Paúl and Sheinerman reported from Washington.

item.title: Bove misled lawmakers about his actions in NYC mayor case, evidence suggests
item.description:
The details from a whistleblower complaint emerged hours before a final vote on Bove’s nomination to a federal judgeship.

Emil Bove misled lawmakers in his confirmation hearings for a federal judgeship when he denied targeting prosecutors who refused to go along with his dismissal of corruption charges against New York Mayor Eric Adams, according to a whistleblower’s documentation of a tense staff meeting.

At the virtual meeting in February, Bove warned public corruption lawyers of the need to follow the “chain of command” in the Adams case, suggesting promotions for lawyers who helped him dismiss the charges and “consequences” for those who didn’t, according to the documentation and two other people familiar with it, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss materials that have not been made public. The Washington Post reviewed the evidence and withheld more details to protect the whistleblower’s identity.

Bove, a former defense attorney for President Donald Trump and current top Justice Department official, was nominated by the president in June for a lifetime seat on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit. He was asked several times by Democratic lawmakers in a contentious confirmation hearing last month whether he ever suggested he would treat prosecutors differently depending on whether they agreed to back the dismissal of the case.

His answers each time were “no” or “I don’t recall.”

The latest disclosures came just hours before a final Senate Judiciary Committee vote on Bove’s nomination Tuesday night, when he was confirmed 50-49. They marked the third whistleblower complaint in recent weeks raising questions about Bove’s forthrightness in answering questions from Senate Democrats, who focused on his role in firing career prosecutors and crafting legal strategy on immigration.

Two other Justice Department whistleblowers have said that Bove told subordinates in a meeting in March that they may need to ignore court orders that would hamper Trump’s campaign to deport millions of undocumented immigrants. One of those whistleblowers, ousted Justice Department attorney Erez Reuveni, has since gone public with his account, quoting Bove as saying, “Justice Department attorneys may have to tell judges ‘f--- you’ and ignore court orders to achieve Trump’s immigration goals.”

The Justice Department and Bove have denied that account, and the White House remained steadfast behind his nomination.

The Adams case was a particular flash point. Bove instructed prosecutors to drop public corruption charges against the Democratic mayor, saying the case was interfering with his ability to govern and efforts to work with the Trump administration on immigration enforcement. The mayor and Justice Department officials denied that Bove proposed a quid pro quo in exchange for Adams carrying out Trump’s wishes.

Before Bove’s Feb. 14 meeting with public integrity prosecutors, the acting U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York and five supervisors who oversaw the public integrity section quit rather than support the dismissal. Several accused Trump’s appointees of acting for political, rather than legal, reasons.

At issue were Bove’s answers to lawmakers about that meeting. The Post has previously reported that Bove told the staff that he needed two people in the office to sign a motion to dismiss the charges and gave them one hour to decide among themselves who would agree, according to multiple accounts of the discussion.

Under questioning in his Senate Judiciary Committee confirmation from Sen. Dick Durbin, (D-Illinois), Bove specifically denied suggesting he would fire or treat anyone differently based on their refusal or agreement to sign.

“On your call with individuals in the public integrity section, did you state, suggest or imply that the section’s career attorneys could be fired if none of them agreed to sign the brief dismissing Mayor Adams’ indictment?” Durbin asked.

“No,” Bove said.

“Did you state, suggest or imply that any individual who agreed to sign the brief would be rewarded?” Durbin asked him.

“I’m sorry, I don’t follow the question,” Bove said.

“Well, you needed somebody to sign that brief … was there any suggestion they be treated any differently because of it?” Durbin asked.

“No,” Bove responded.

But people familiar with the meeting said Bove specifically mentioned that people who agreed to sign the motion might become “leaders” in the office.

Ed Sullivan, the single trial lawyer from the section who ultimately signed the motion, was later promoted to become head of the section.

Senate Democrats spent weeks trying to persuade Republicans to sink Bove’s nomination for the court, which takes cases from Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware and the Virgin Islands. They argued he would prioritize the president’s agenda over properly enforcing the law and complained Republicans have ignored the whistleblower complaints.

Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey), a Judiciary Committee member, and other Democrats reviewed the evidence, multiple Senate staffers told The Post.

“We have substantial information relevant to the truthfulness of the nominee,” Booker said in a speech on the Senate floor ahead of a preliminary vote on Bove’s nomination. At the time, he invited his Republican colleagues to review the claims. None immediately took him up on his offer, Senate staffers said.

The staff of Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) met Monday with the whistleblower’s lawyers after days of back and forth and reviewed a summary of the allegations, according to his spokeswoman Clare Slattery. But Grassley’s staff was not allowed to review the underlying evidence, and Booker never approached Grassley directly about it, she said.

“These eleventh-hour allegations, which were shared in advance with Democrats and the media but not with the Chairman or his staff, reek of a bad-faith attempt to sink a nominee who’s already received committee approval,” Slattery said in a statement.

Aaron Schaffer and Alice Crites contributed to this report.

item.title: New details emerge in New York City shooting investigation
item.description:
Four people were killed, including a police officer, and one was seriously injured when a gunman opened fire inside an office building before killing himself.

Authorities investigating Monday’s fatal shooting inside a Manhattan office building are focusing on a note left by the gunman, Shane Tamura, New York Mayor Eric Adams said. Speaking to MSNBC on Tuesday morning, Adams said the note referenced CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a disease linked to head trauma, and that Tamura appeared to be “focused on the NFL,” which has offices in the 44-story building at 345 Park Avenue.

Police say the 27-year-old from Las Vegas, who had a “documented mental health history,” traveled across the country before entering the lobby of the skyscraper with an AR-style rifle and “spraying it with gunfire.” He then went to the 33rd floor, where he fired more rounds and fatally shot himself, police said. He killed four people, including a police officer, an investment company worker and a security guard, and injured an NFL employee.

Here’s what to know about the attack.

What do we know about the shooting in New York?

The deadly incident began just before 6:30 p.m., when a black BMW double-parked on one of New York City’s busiest streets. The gunman stepped out of the car holding a rifle, according to New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch, who cautioned that the recounting of events was “preliminary and subject to change.”

The gunman walked into the building through the main entrance. Inside the lobby, he turned right and “immediately” opened fire on off-duty New York City police officer Didarul Islam, Tisch said, citing surveillance video.

The gunman also shot a woman who tried to take cover behind a pillar, then proceeded through the lobby, “spraying it with gunfire,” Tisch said. He hit a security guard taking cover behind the security desk. Another man was shot in the lobby, according to his statement from the hospital, the police commissioner said.

The shooter called an elevator, and when it arrived, he allowed a woman to walk past him, unharmed. He headed to the 33rd floor, where he fatally shot a second woman before turning his weapon on himself. The office of Rudin Management, a real estate firm that manages the building, is on that floor, Tisch said.

While police have not confirmed the shooter’s motive, Adams told MSNBC’s “Morning Joe” on Tuesday that authorities had “reason to believe that he was focused on the NFL agency that was located in the building.”

“From our preliminary investigation, he took the wrong elevator bank up to the NFL headquarters,” Adams told CBS News. “Instead, it took him to Rudin Management. And that is where he carried out additional shootings and took the lives of additional employees.”

“He did have a note on him,” Adams said. “The note alluded to that he felt he had CTE, a known brain injury for those who participate in contact sports. He appeared to have blamed the NFL for his injury.”

CTE can be diagnosed definitively only after death.

What do we know about the victims?

All four of the victims who were fatally shot have been identified.

Islam, 36, the NYPD officer, was an immigrant from Bangladesh who had been on the force for 3½ years, authorities said. He was assigned to the 47th Precinct in the Bronx but was working off-duty at 345 Park Ave. through a program that allows companies to hire uniformed officers to provide security, Tisch said. Islam had two young boys, and his wife is pregnant with the couple’s third child.

“He was doing the job that we asked him to do,” Tisch said. “He put himself in harm’s way. He made the ultimate sacrifice, shot in cold blood, wearing a uniform that stood for the promise that he made to this city. He died, as he lived, a hero.”

Adams said he had met with Islam’s family before the news conference to offer his sympathies.

“He embodies what this city is all about,” the mayor said. “He’s a true-blue New Yorker, not only in the uniform he wore, but in spirit and energy of loving this city.”

Investment firm Blackstone, which has an office in the building where the attack took place, said Tuesday morning that it was “heartbroken to share that our colleague, Wesley LePatner, was among those who lost their lives.”

“Words cannot express the devastation we feel,” the company said in an emailed statement. “Wesley was a beloved member of the Blackstone family and will be sorely missed. She was brilliant, passionate, warm, generous, and deeply respected within our firm and beyond. … Our prayers are with her husband, children and family.”

The Service Employees International Union identified 46-year-old Aland Etienne, a guard at the building employed by McLane Security, as a third victim. He was in charge of the building’s elevators, Adams said, and was killed at the security desk. His union president called him “a New York hero.”

Julia Hyman, a 2020 graduate of Cornell University, was an associate at Rudin Management, the school confirmed Tuesday. She had visited her alma mater’s campus this summer for a five-year reunion with classmates.

Hyman studied hotel and restaurant administration, with a minor in real estate at the school, where her older sister also attended. Hyman left a “lasting impression” at the university with her “determination, warmth, and a strong commitment to learning,” professor Kate Walsh recalled in a statement shared by the university.

The NFL employee injured in Monday’s shooting, Craig Clementi, works in the league’s finance department, a person with knowledge of the situation said. Doctors expect him to recover from his injuries, according to another person familiar with the matter. Both spoke on the condition of anonymity because the authorities and the NFL had not confirmed the employee’s identity.

Clementi’s father-in-law, Robert Hunter, told the New York Daily News that Clementi “was on his way home when he got shot.” He “came through the surgery and there was some spinal damage,” but he is “doing well,” Hunter said.

Who was the gunman?

Authorities identified the gunman as Shane Tamura, 27, of Las Vegas. According to Tisch, the gunman had a gun license from Nevada. He also had a “documented mental health history,” she said.

A New York Police Department spokesperson said the department found a handwritten three-page missive in his wallet, which they described as a suicide note. According to excerpts provided by police, he wrote on the first page: “Study my brain please” and “I’m sorry.”

The gunman played high school football and did not reach the NFL, although he appeared to blame the league in his note. Officials believe he had homed in on the NFL ahead of the attack, but they have not disclosed an exact motive.

“Football gave me CTE,” Tamura wrote in the note, according to police.

The last job he worked was in overnight security at the Horseshoe Las Vegas casino. He was scheduled to work last Sunday but did not show up for his shift, Tisch said in a recorded statement Tuesday.

Investigators en route to Nevada will conduct interviews, search the gunman’s home and visit the store where the weapon he used was purchased, according to Tisch. The AR-style rifle was purchased by an associate of the shooter whom officials have located, Tisch said. She did not identify that person or any other people whom investigators may be questioning.

Those efforts, Tisch said, would give a “detailed picture of how and why this happened.”

The gunman appeared to have driven across the country in recent days, traveling through Colorado on Saturday and then Nebraska and Iowa on Sunday, Tisch said. An initial investigation showed he was in Columbia, New Jersey, at 4:24 p.m. and drove into New York City shortly afterward.

Bomb squad technicians checked the shooter’s BMW for explosives but did not discover any, Tisch said. Inside the vehicle, police found a rifle case with a loaded revolver, ammunition, a backpack and medication prescribed to Tamura.

“There are still many questions that we have to answer, and we will answer them,” Tisch said. “But for now, our city is in mourning for the innocent lives lost. May their memories be a blessing.”

Jacobs reported from New York. Marie-Rose Sheinerman contributed to this report.

item.title: Authorities investigating NYC gunman’s note that referenced CTE and NFL, NYPD says
item.description:
NEW YORK — Three of the four victims have been identified in Monday’s shooting inside a Manhattan office building. Authorities are investigating a note left by the gunman, Shane Tamura, according to Mayor Eric Adams. He said in TV interviews that the note referenced chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a disease linked to head trauma, and that Tamura incorrectly believed he was a former player in the NFL, which has offices in the building.

Police say the 27-year-old from Las Vegas, who had “documented mental health history,” traveled across the country before entering the lobby of the skyscraper armed with a rifle and “spraying it with gunfire.” He then went to the 33rd floor, where he fired more rounds and shot himself to death. He killed four people, including a police officer, and injured an NFL employee.



Tuesday, July 29, 2025 3:52 PM EDT

Slain security guard Aland Etienne was ‘a light in our lives,’ brother says

By María Luisa Paúl

Gathmand Etienne mourned the death of his brother Aland Etienne, a security guard who was shot while behind his desk after a gunman burst into the lobby of the Midtown building Monday.

“He was more than a brother — he was a father, a son, and a light in our lives,” Gathmand Etienne wrote on Facebook. “Our hearts are shattered, and we’re asking for your prayers and strength as we navigate this painful time.”

He added that his brother will “never be forgotten.”

Tuesday, July 29, 2025 3:47 PM EDT

New York ‘is wounded’ and mourning, governor says

By Praveena Somasundaram

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) called on elected officials to find the “courage” to push stronger gun legislation nationwide while her state mourns the four people who were fatally shot in a Midtown Manhattan skyscraper.

“Our state is wounded right now,” Hochul said in a CNN interview Tuesday. “We’re hurting.”

Hochul said she would be at a vigil for the shooting victims, whose families she plans to meet with. She added that she would visit the New York Police Department’s 47th precinct, where slain Officer Didarul Islam worked. The precinct is closed Tuesday, giving those who knew and worked with Islam time to grieve, Hochul said.

She urged lawmakers across the country to support national and state-level assault weapon bans, which New York has enacted. Had other states — such as Nevada, where the gunman reportedly acquired the AR-15 style rifle he used in the shooting — enacted such legislation, it would have been harder for individuals to carry out mass violence, Hochul said.

“That sense of security is shattered when someone comes from another state carrying an assault weapon designed only for battlefields, but intending to use that to commit mayhem and mass murder in our city,” she said.



Tuesday, July 29, 2025 3:42 PM EDT

Officer killed in Midtown shooting is honored

By Washington Post staff

The ambulance carrying the body of Didarul Islam exits New York-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell Medical Center during a dignified transfer ceremony early Tuesday in New York.

New York Police Department officers bring out the body of Islam, who was killed by a gunman Monday evening.

Members of the New York Fire Department place a banner outside the 47th Precinct, Islam’s home police station.



Tuesday, July 29, 2025 3:18 PM EDT

Gunman’s AR-15-style rifle is an increasingly common sight

By Todd C. Frankel

The gunman used an AR-15-style rifle, police said.

AR-15-style guns are the best-selling rifles in America. They were once rare and even widely considered taboo, but millions of people own one today — in some cases, many more than one.

This is an excerpt from a full story.

By Gaya Gupta

A multifaith vigil will be held at Bryant Park at 8 p.m. Tuesday to honor the four victims of the shooting, Mayor Eric Adams announced on social media. “We will get through this together as a city,” he wrote.



Tuesday, July 29, 2025 2:48 PM EDT

What is CTE, the brain disease linked to head trauma, contact sports?

By Annabelle Timsit

A man who opened fire inside a Manhattan office building and fatally shot four people left a note referencing chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a neurodegenerative disease linked to head trauma, New York Mayor Eric Adams confirmed Tuesday.

This is an excerpt from a full story.

Tuesday, July 29, 2025 2:13 PM EDT

Police found three-page note in gunman’s wallet

By Praveena Somasundaram

A New York Police Department spokesperson said the department found a three-page, handwritten missive in the wallet of Shane Tamura, the gunman who shot and killed four people in a Park Avenue skyscraper Monday night, which they described as a suicide note.

According to excerpts provided by police, Tamura wrote on the first page: “Study my brain please” and “I’m sorry.”

On all three pages, Tamura made references to CTE, chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a degenerative brain disease known to affect athletes, and military and combat veterans. Tamura, a former high school football player, also made references to the NFL, though he did not play for the league. Officials believe Tamura had homed in on the NFL ahead of the attack, but they have not yet disclosed an exact motive.

“Football gave me CTE,” Tamura wrote in the note, according to police.

On the note’s last page, he again wrote “I’m sorry” and lashed out at the NFL.

“The league knowingly concealed the dangers to our brains to maximize profits,” Tamura wrote. “They failed us.”

Tuesday, July 29, 2025 1:53 PM EDT

Where the shooting took place

By Victoria Craw

The shooting took place at 345 Park Avenue, a 44-story building that occupies a whole block in Manhattan’s Midtown and was opened in 1969, according to property management company Rudin, which has offices at the site. It’s also home to offices of investment management company Blackstone, the National Football League and professional services network KPMG.

An NFL staff member was “seriously injured” in the attack, according to a message to staff from NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell. Staff based at the site were told to work remotely on Tuesday or take the day off if necessary. There will also be an increased security presence at the site in the days and weeks to come, Goodell said.



Tuesday, July 29, 2025 1:31 PM EDT

Slain officer’s friends grieve a ‘humble,’ ‘hard-working’ man

By El Calabrese

THE BRONX — Didarul Islam, the police officer killed Monday, was “a very hard-working person,” said Abdul Salaman, whose friendship with Islam began when the two lived in Bangladesh and continued when both came to live in the Bronx.

“We grew up together,” Salaman said. As he left the home where Islam lived with his pregnant wife and two children, Salaman added that “they are very sad, everybody.” An NYPD vehicle was parked outside the building.

Across the street, P.S. 47 — the local elementary school — displayed a tribute to “our loving parent and NYPD Hero Didarul Islam.”

“Heroes, in their quiet grace, leave in our world, a brighter trace,” read a poem included on the sign, which was decorated with blue and white carnations and tied to a fence.

Tanjim Talukder, 29, said he and Islam would walk to the Bronx’s Parkchester Islamic Center together on Fridays around 1 p.m. and talk about politics in Bangladesh. The neighborhood’s Bangladeshi community is a close one, he said.

“I used to see him a lot on the street,” Talukder said of Islam, recalling that the officer and his family would frequent restaurants on Sterling Avenue.

“He was a friendly guy, humble,” Talukder said. “I feel so sad.”



Tuesday, July 29, 2025 1:19 PM EDT

New York gunman appeared to target NFL, had mental health history

By Vivian Ho

The gunman who opened fire inside a high-rise office building in Midtown Manhattan was a 27-year-old Las Vegas resident with a “documented mental health history,” authorities said.

This is an excerpt from a full story. Tuesday, July 29, 2025 12:58 PM EDT

Adams: Shooter believed he was an ex-NFL player

By Gaya Gupta

Mayor Eric Adams shared details Tuesday about the ongoing investigation into Shane Tamura, whom authorities have identified as the suspected shooter.

Adams told CNN’s Wolf Blitzer that the suspected shooter’s motive appeared to be connected to his belief that he was suffering from CTE, a neurodegenerative disease commonly associated with former athletes, and that he was an ex-NFL player, which the mayor confirmed was untrue. Police also found large numbers of bullets in the car, he said, but concluded that he did not have plans to inflict further violence.

When asked whether an autopsy would be performed and whether Tamura would be tested for CTE, Adams said the city’s Medical Examiner’s office would decide next steps with Manhattan County’s District Attorney; examination of the brain, a neuropathology, is part of a complete autopsy, according to New York’s Office of Chief Medical Examiner.

“There are many layers of investigation that we have to peel back to sort of get a full understanding of what took place here and what motivated the shooting of this magnitude,” he said.

Adams said two teams would be sent to Las Vegas to execute a search warrant and trace the two firearms that were recovered.

Tamura was “not on our radar at all,” Adams said, adding that Tamura had a permit to obtain firearms, but the teams sent to Las Vegas would be looking into whether the firearms were legally possessed and whether they were on his permit. He lauded his own administration’s efforts in removing illegal guns and weapons off New York’s streets, and pointed out that the firearm “came into our city” and other jurisdictions have more lax gun policies.

“We really need to look at allowing our federal law enforcement officials to look into the database of those with severe mental health illness. Should they be allowed to carry firearms? This is a conversation that is going to be carried out on the federal level,” he said.



By Mark Maske

The NFL employee injured in Monday’s shooting, Craig Clementi, works in the league’s finance department, a person with knowledge of the situation said. Doctors expect him to recover from his injuries, according to another person familiar with the matter. Both spoke on the condition of anonymity because the authorities and NFL have not confirmed the employee’s identity.

Clementi’s father-in-law, Robert Hunter, told the New York Daily News that Clementi “was on his way home when he got shot.” He “came through the surgery and there was some spinal damage” but he is “doing well,” Hunter said.



Tuesday, July 29, 2025 12:31 PM EDT

Union identifies slain security guard, calls him ‘a New York hero’

By Kim Bellware

The security guard killed in Monday’s shooting in Manhattan was Aland Etienne, according to Manny Pastreich, president of 32BJ SEIU, one of New York’s largest unions representing workers including security guards, doormen and janitors.

Police said Etienne was shot while behind his security desk after a gunman burst into the lobby of the Midtown building.

Pastreich in a statement described Etienne as a dedicated employee “who took his job duties extremely seriously.” Etienne, Pastreich said, was “a New York hero.”

“We will remember him as such.”

Tuesday, July 29, 2025 12:24 PM EDT

CTE has been found in former high school players, expert says

By Rick Maese

While chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is often associated with prolonged professional football careers and years of repeated exposure to head trauma, the degenerative brain disease has been diagnosed in young athletes whose football careers never advanced beyond the high school field.

In an interview Tuesday, Ann McKee, the director of Boston University’s CTE Center, said she would not be surprised to discover that Shane Tamura was suffering from the effects of CTE when he opened fire in a Manhattan office building Monday. Police say Tamura referenced CTE in a note discovered by police.

“I do think it’s possible he has CTE because we have seen it in former high school players with just that amount of exposure,” McKee said. “Of course, it’s more common in individuals who play longer periods of football, but it is possible. It’s also possible he has a mental health disorder.”

McKee is among the world’s leading CTE researchers and co-wrote a 2023 study that found 41 percent of former amateur athletes who were 30 or younger at the time of death had evidence of CTE. McKee notes there was selection bias associated with the study and the numbers probably don’t reflect the general population of athletes. But the study did show that young athletes are susceptible to the disease and that the pathology of CTE can start early.

McKee is the neuropathologist credited with some of the most high-profile CTE diagnoses, including former athletes who were prone to violence, such as Aaron Hernandez, the former NFL tight end who was serving a life sentence for murder when he killed himself in 2017, and Phillip Adams, a 32-year old former NFL player who killed seven people, including himself, in 2021.

“There is some precedent linking individuals with known CTE and rampages of violence,” McKee said. “We’ve seen it in young players, former football players.” She explained that damage to the frontal lobe caused by repeated blows to the head could result in impulsivity, poor judgment or violent outbursts.

It is not known what types of injuries Tamura might have suffered during his high school playing career in Southern California. Tamura referenced CTE in a note he apparently wrote before killing four people and then himself Monday, authorities said.

One former high school teammate of Tamura’s said in an interview Tuesday he could not recall Tamura suffering any injuries during his senior season at Granada Hills Charter.

McKee was not certain of the fate of Tamura’s brain and whether it would end up in her brain bank for study, noting that it is likely to belong to the medical examiner for the time being.



Tuesday, July 29, 2025 12:16 PM EDT

Getting a gun is much easier in Nevada than New York

By Ben Brasch

It is much easier to obtain a gun in Nevada, where shooter Shane Tamura was living, than it is in New York.

Nevada has no gun owner licensing, no assault-weapon restrictions, no ban on large-capacity magazines and no open-carry regulations, according to gun-control advocacy group Giffords. Meanwhile, the state of New York has all those things and other regulations.

Officials say Tamura made the 2,500-mile drive from Nevada to New York. The Transportation Security Administration has strict rules around flying with a firearm.

Authorities have not yet disclosed how Tamura acquired his gun.

Nevada runs its own gun licensing instead of using the federal National Instant Criminal Background Check System. The Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department did not immediately respond to questions about whether the agency had issued Tamura had a concealed-carry permit.

The Nevada Private Investigators Licensing Board issued a five-year private investigators license to a “Shane Devon Tamura” in December 2019. The firearm status on the license was listed as “no.” The Board’s office did not immediately respond to an early-morning request to confirm that the license was issued to the same Tamura who police say killed four people at a Manhattan office building.

Nevada recognizes gun permits from most other states, according to the National Rifle Association. New York only recognizes its own permit, according to the NRA.



Tuesday, July 29, 2025 11:47 AM EDT

Photos: The Midtown shooting scene

Members of the NYPD Crime Scene Unit inspect shattered glass at the scene of a deadly mass shooting in Manhattan on Tuesday.

A man raises the U.S. flag half-staff Tuesday near the scene of the mass shooting in Manhattan.

By Praveena Somasundaram

Former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo, a candidate in New York City’s mayoral race, commemorated Officer Didarul Islam in a statement Tuesday, calling him a hero who had courage “as boundless as his love for the city.”

“We honor his sacrifice and the quiet bravery of every NYPD officer who stands the watch so we can live free,” Cuomo said.



By Rachel Hatzipanagos

The New York City offices of investment company Blackstone will be closed today, said an employee with the company who declined to be named. One employee from Blackstone, Wesley LePatner, was among those killed, the company said in a statement.



Tuesday, July 29, 2025 10:43 AM EDT

There have been 7 mass killings with guns in 2025

By Washington Post staff

Since 2006, guns have been used in an average of 25 mass killings per year in the United States, killing 2,584 people in all. We use the term “mass killing” to describe events in which four or more people died, not including the perpetrators. These violent episodes have occurred seven times since the beginning of 2025.

This is an excerpt from a full story.

By Praveena Somasundaram

The Los Angeles Police Department is investigating whether the gunman in the Midtown Manhattan shooting had any connection to the agency, a spokesperson said. Online rumors and questions from reporters prompted the probe, the spokesperson said, but as of Tuesday morning, the department did not yet have any confirmed details to share publicly.



By Mark Maske

The building at 345 Park Ave. is set back from the street, with a large area in front that includes seating and often draws lunchtime crowds. The lobby has entrances from multiple sides.

There is a security desk, generally with multiple security staffers seated there, at which any visitors must stop and be approved to enter. The elevators are near the security desk.



Tuesday, July 29, 2025 10:04 AM EDT

New York governor calls for national assault weapons ban

By Praveena Somasundaram

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) criticized nationwide gun legislation, saying her state’s strong gun laws alone could not prevent people from accessing military-style weapons and carrying out attacks.

Officials have said the gunman drove cross-country from Las Vegas, making it to New York on Monday before opening fire in a New York skyscraper. New York bans certain military-style weapons and bars people from carrying weapons in sensitive locations, such as schools and parks.

“Our laws only go so far when an AR-15 can be obtained in a state with weak gun laws and brought into New York to commit mass murder,” Hochul wrote in a statement Tuesday about the Midtown Manhattan shooting.

The governor described the shooting as a “horrific act of violence” that killed one of New York’s police officers, Didarul Islam, a 3½-year veteran of the department who leaves behind two young sons and a wife pregnant with their third child.

To honor Islam and the other three victims, Hochul on Tuesday directed all of New York’s government buildings to fly flags at half-staff. The flags will remain there until all of the victims have been laid to rest, Hochul said.

Tuesday, July 29, 2025 9:37 AM EDT

Adams: Safe rooms in building helped save lives

By Victoria Craw

New York Mayor Eric Adams said safe rooms with bulletproof doors at 345 Park Avenue allowed some people to shelter during the shooting attack on Monday evening and that authorities believe “it played a major role in not having a greater loss of life.”

The building, operated by property management company Rudin, contained “so many safeguards,” Adams said in an interview with MSNBC’s Morning Joe on Tuesday, including a block on the elevator, though the “security guard that was in charge of that operation was killed at the desk.”

“There were safe rooms, such as the bathrooms, where you had bulletproof doors, and you were able to lock in the staffers inside,” Adams said, adding that “several individuals” were able to do so.



By Amy B Wang

President Donald Trump said he has been briefed on the shooting that took place Monday in a Midtown Manhattan office building.

“I trust our Law Enforcement Agencies to get to the bottom of why this crazed lunatic committed such a senseless act of violence,” Trump wrote on his social media platform Tuesday. “My heart is with the families of the four people who were killed, including the NYPD Officer, who made the ultimate sacrifice. God Bless the New York Police Department, and God Bless New York!”



Tuesday, July 29, 2025 8:56 AM EDT

Suspect appeared ‘focused on the NFL’ and referenced CTE in note, mayor says

By Victoria Craw

New York Mayor Eric Adams said police are investigating a note from the suspected gunman and potential links to the NFL and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a neurodegenerative disease linked to head trauma.

Speaking on MSNBC’s “Morning Joe” on Tuesday morning, Adams was asked by anchor Willie Geist about a note from the shooter, Shane Tamura, and whether he mentioned CTE.

“We’re still investigating, this is relatively new,” Adams said. “There’s no more than just a note at this time and as you indicated he talked about CTE.”

Adams said the gunman was not an NFL player but authorities had “reason to believe that he was focused on the NFL agency that was located in the building.”

CTE can pose a threat to athletes who receive blows to the head, according to the National Institutes of Health. It can lead to dementia and death.

By Victoria Bisset

The day before the rampage, New York Mayor Eric Adams said shootings in the city in the first six months of the year were at “record lows.” Last year “was the fourth-lowest year for shootings in New York City in recorded history,” he said Sunday, adding that “2025 is on track to be even safer.”



By Victoria Bisset

Investment company Blackstone confirmed Tuesday that its employee Wesley LePatner was among those killed. “Words cannot express the devastation we feel. Wesley was a beloved member of the Blackstone family and will be sorely missed,” the company said in an emailed statement. “She was brilliant, passionate, warm, generous, and deeply respected within our firm and beyond. She embodied the best of Blackstone. Our prayers are with her husband, children and family.”



By Victoria Bisset

New York Mayor Eric Adams ordered flags on all city buildings and stationary flagstaffs to be fly at half-staff until further notice, as “a mark of respect for the memory of NYPD Officer Didarul Islam who died in the line of duty” and the other victims of Monday evening’s shooting in Midtown Manhattan.

By Victoria Bisset

Zohran Mamdani, New York’s Democratic mayoral nominee, paid tribute to Didarul Islam, the police officer killed in Monday’s shooting. “When he joined the police department, his mother asked him why he would pursue such a dangerous job. He told her it was to leave behind a legacy that his family could be proud of,” Mamdani wrote. “He has done that, and more. I pray for him, his family, and honor the legacy of service and sacrifice he leaves behind.”



Tuesday, July 29, 2025 4:05 AM EDT

What we know about the New York City shooting so far

By Michael E. Miller, Frances Vinall, Andrew Jeong and Shayna Jacobs

Four people were killed, including a New York City police officer, and one seriously injured when a gunman opened fire inside a high-rise office building in Midtown Manhattan on Monday evening.

The gunman then fatally shot himself in the chest, New York City Police Commissioner Jessica S. Tisch said at a news conference Monday night. The attack put the 44-story building into lockdown and threw a normally busy rush hour in the United States’ most populous city into chaos.

This is an excerpt from a full story.

By Michael E. Miller

An NFL employee was “seriously injured” in this attack, according to an all-staff message sent by NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell. The male employee was in the hospital in stable condition on Monday night and all other employees were safe and accounted for, according to the email, which was obtained by The Washington Post.

Tuesday, July 29, 2025 1:35 AM EDT

New York leaders express sorrow for slain victims, including NYPD officer

By Andrew Jeong

New York leaders expressed pain and anger late Monday as authorities briefed reporters at a news conference about the victims, which included an NYPD officer, and details of what unfolded in Midtown Manhattan earlier that evening.

A somber-faced New York Mayor Eric Adams, a former NYPD officer himself, needed a long pause before he started his remarks. “This never gets easy,” he said as he talked about Didarul Islam, the slain police officer who was a father of two, with a third child on the way.

“Early tonight, I met with the officer’s family, told them that he was a hero,” Adams said.

“I think about Jordan, my child, and it’s unimaginable to experience a loss of this magnitude,” he added.

Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) said Islam “represented the very best of New York,” as an immigrant who had joined the New York police force “to protect his city — and gave his life doing so.”

“We hold his family in our prayers tonight,” she said in a post on X.

Rep. Dan Goldman (D-New York), whose district includes Lower Manhattan, expressed anger.

“This isn’t about New York. This is about Republicans persistently blocking common sense gun safety reform,” he said in a post on X.

The post came in response to remarks from Vivek Ramaswamy, the former Republican presidential candidate, who said the tragedy was the result of “weak leadership and anti-cop policies,” in a post on X.

Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-New York) praised Islam as a “brave NYPD hero who ran into the rampage to save people’s lives from the violent, murderous criminal in Midtown Manhattan,” in a post on X.



REPORTING FROM NEW YORK

By Shayna Jacobs

Slain NYPD Officer Didarul Islam was transported out of the hospital early Tuesday with members of the police department, the mayor and police officials saluting him as his body was moved to a transport vehicle on a gurney. There appeared to be members of his family following his body out of the hospital.



By Frances Vinall

New York Mayor Eric Adams (D) said early Tuesday that he was en route for the “dignified transfer” of NYPD Officer Didarul Islam, who was killed at 345 Park Ave. on Monday. “He put his life on the line for all of us and died a hero,” Adams said. Islam had earlier been transported to New York-Presbyterian Hospital.

Tuesday, July 29, 2025 12:44 AM EDT

Gunman fired at victims in lobby, 33rd floor before shooting himself

By Frances Vinall

The gunman, who police identified as 27-year-old Shane Tamura, walked into the Midtown Manhattan building’s lobby Monday carrying an M4 rifle, turned right and immediately fired at NYPD officer Didarul Islam, New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch told reporters, in a recounting of events that she cautioned was “preliminary and subject to change.” Tamura then shot a woman who had taken cover behind a pillar, she said.

While walking toward an elevator bank, he sprayed the lobby with gunfire and shot a security guard taking cover behind a desk and another man. Tamura then entered an elevator as a woman, who was unharmed, exited, and he went to the 33rd floor, where the office of the Rudin Management Company, the real estate management and development firm that manages the building, is located, Tisch said.

As he walked around the floor, Tamura fired rounds, killing one person, before shooting himself in the chest, she said.

Before the shooting, he had exited a black BMW that was double-parked on Park Ave. between 51st and 52nd streets, according to Tisch. Authorities found a rifle case with rounds, a loaded revolver, ammunition and magazines, as well as a backpack and medication prescribed to Tamura in the vehicle, which was registered in Nevada in Tamura’s name.

Tisch said the vehicle had been driven cross-country, through Colorado on Saturday, Nebraska and Iowa on Sunday, and entered New York City late Monday afternoon, citing an initial investigation. Calls to 911 began coming in about the shooting at 6:28 p.m., she said.



By Michael E. Miller

New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said the gunman had a weapons license in Nevada, where he lived, and a “documented mental health history.” She said the initial investigation showed that he had driven across the country in recent days, only entering New York City shortly before the shooting.



By Andrew Jeong

Authorities believe the shooter was Shane Tamura, a 27-year-old man with a Las Vegas address, New York City Police Commissioner Jessica S. Tisch told reporters. The vehicle he was seen exiting before the shooting is registered in Nevada and inside, investigators found a rifle case with rounds, a loaded revolver, ammunition in magazines, a backpack and medication, she said.

REPORTING FROM NEW YORK

By Shayna Jacobs

The slain NYPD officer was Didarul Islam, who worked in a Bronx precinct but was at a paid detail at the Midtown building, according to police.



By Andrew Jeong

New York City Police Commissioner Jessica S. Tisch told reporters late Monday that there is no longer an active threat to the public and that authorities believe the gunman who was found dead was a lone shooter.



By Andrew Jeong

The gunman killed at least four people before he was also found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound, New York Mayor Eric Adams (D) said at a news conference late Monday. The deceased include NYPD officer Didarul Islam, 36, as well as two men and one woman, whose names were not released. Another man, who was also not named, is in critical condition, Adams said.

By Bart Schaneman

New York Mayor Eric Adams (D) and New York Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch are expected to speak at a news conference soon.



By Marie-Rose Sheinerman

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) wrote on X that she had been briefed on the situation. “Please avoid the area of 52nd St. between Park and 3rd Ave at this time,” she said.



By Marie-Rose Sheinerman

Agents from the FBI’s New York field office were responding to the site to provide support, FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino said.

item.title: What is CTE, the brain disease linked to head trauma, contact sports?
item.description:
New York Mayor Eric Adams said a note from the shooting suspect mentioned chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a brain disease associated with repeated brain injuries.

A man who opened fire inside a Manhattan office building and fatally shot four people left a note referencing chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a neurodegenerative disease linked to head trauma, New York Mayor Eric Adams confirmed Tuesday.

“There’s no more than just a note at this time, and as you indicated he talked about CTE,” Adams said in response to a question from MSNBC anchor Willie Geist about the note left by the suspected shooter whom authorities have identified as Shane Tamura, 27.

It is not clear if the gunman suffered from CTE, which is commonly associated with former athletes who have suffered repeated brain injuries. But authorities had “reason to believe that he was focused on the NFL agency that was located in the building,” he said.

Here’s what to know about CTE.

What is CTE, and what are its symptoms?

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, is a degenerative brain disease that is caused by repetitive hits to the head and has been associated with contact sports, such as football and boxing. It is marked by accumulations of an abnormal or defective form of a protein called tau in the brain.

According to clinicians, while CTE is a specific condition, some of its symptoms are similar to those seen in people with other forms of dementia, including Alzheimer’s disease. They include memory loss, confusion, depression and anxiety. People with CTE may also have trouble sleeping and controlling impulses, and can exhibit erratic behavior, according to the Weill Institute for Neurosciences at the University of California at San Francisco.

The disease was discovered in the 1920s but has been studied in more depth only since the early 2000s, when researchers discovered signs of it in former athletes who played popular contact sports. Many aspects of it — from its cause to possible treatments — remain the subject of debate, according to Richard Sylvester, a consultant neurologist at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery in London, who works with former athletes with acute traumatic brain injuries.

Scientists believe that repetitive brain trauma — not just concussions, but also less severe blows — is a precondition for CTE. But not everyone who sustains repeated brain trauma develops CTE, and symptoms can develop years after a person’s last traumatic brain injury.

When was CTE discovered?

The condition was first described in 1928 by a New Jersey pathologist named Harrison Martland. In a paper, Martland described how boxing fans and promoters had noticed how athletes who sustained “considerable head punishment” were developing symptoms that made them appear “punch drunk.”

Over the next 70 years, doctors encountered similar symptoms in boxers, and the syndrome became commonly known as “dementia pugilistica.”

In 2005, a pathologist named Bennet Omalu reported finding widespread brain damage for the first time in a former NFL player, Mike Webster. The discovery was initially ignored, but it later inspired an avalanche of scientific research that prompted the NFL to acknowledge a link between football and brain disease.

How is CTE treated?

There is no known cure for CTE. Doctors typically prescribe medication to treat its symptoms, including mood and behavior changes, according to the Weill Institute.

A key part of any treatment program is management of the patient’s mental and physical health, said Nathan Howarth, executive director of the Concussion Legacy Foundation in Britain. Medications can be used to stabilize moods, and doctors will often look to treat any physical conditions contributing to poor sleep, such as sleep apnea, and overall poor health, such as heart disease, Howarth said. “The fitter your body is, the fitter your brain will be,” he added.

How do doctors test for CTE?

It is not possible to definitively diagnose CTE in people who are alive. The condition is diagnosed after a patient dies. During an autopsy, brain tissue is analyzed, and doctors look for patterns of protein accumulation in the nerve cells. But that process is complicated by the fact that abnormal tau is also found in more than a dozen other diseases. Tau also accumulates in healthy brains as people age, with no apparent effect on brain function or behavior.

In 2014, a group of neuropathologists from around the world developed research diagnostic criteria for the symptoms of CTE, known as traumatic encephalopathy syndrome (TES), in living people. A clinician might use the criteria, alongside a physical examination and assessment of the patient’s medical history, as guidance to determine the likelihood that they have CTE on a scale of “unlikely” to “probable,” said Howarth.

But the TES criteria are more of a research tool than a diagnostic tool, said Sylvester. And aspects of it have evolved as the scientific understanding of CTE has changed. In 2021, for example, the consensus group that developed the TES criteria removed suicidality, as well as mood and anxiety disorders, from the criteria because of their relatively high prevalence in the general population and the risk of false-positives.

A 2021 experiment to test the validity of the criteria found that they provided good evidence to rule out CTE but were limited in their ability to detect CTE pathology.

Who is most likely to sustain CTE?

CTE is commonly associated with athletes who play contact sports such as boxing, football and rugby, because of the higher likelihood that they will suffer repeated traumatic brain injuries over time.

Members of the military and combat veterans are also affected, though there is no comprehensive assessment of how many are likely to suffer from the condition. Howarth says veterans can develop CTE even if they have never been deployed to a combat zone, if they suffer traumatic brain injuries from exposure to blast waves from firing weapons during training, for example.

What is the life expectancy of someone with CTE?

According to the Weill Institute, “a person with CTE can live many years with the disease.” The Cleveland Clinic says in its guidance that the condition isn’t fatal and “won’t affect your life expectancy.”

But its symptoms can progressively worsen over time, and patients can eventually die from a weakened immune system or the end stage of cognitive degeneration, said Sylvester. Individuals with CTE may at some point lose their ability to care for themselves. In extreme cases, people with CTE may no longer be recognizable to their loved ones. They may experience complete changes to their personality, causing them to act more aggressively and inappropriately in social situations, become harder to understand because of speech issues, or have increased difficulty walking and staying balanced, the Weill Institute said.

Will Hobson contributed to this report.

item.title: Alabama’s body-camera law undermines police accountability, lawyers say
item.description:
The case of Jabari Peoples, a Black teen killed by police, has sparked criticism of a 2023 law meant to enhance police accountability.

Jabari Peoples, an 18-year-old college student, was spending time with his girlfriend outside a sports complex in Homewood, Alabama, relatives say, when a police officer approached his car. Within moments, the Black teen was lying on the ground, dying from the officer’s gunshot to his back, according to the family’s independent autopsy.

But what happened in those moments the evening of June 23 is disputed: Officials say Peoples grabbed a gun from his car door during a scuffle with the officer; his family says he was unarmed.

Now, Peoples’s relatives are in a weeks-long standoff with law enforcement over its refusal to release the body-camera recording of the deadly encounter — a battle that centers on a police transparency law sponsored by a Democratic state lawmaker in the wake of Black Lives Matter protests two years ago. The battle has sparked protests and petitions, along with fiercely worded accusations from a civil rights lawyer who says the law’s sponsor, state Rep. Juandalynn Givan (D), has made the path to justice harder for Alabamans harmed by police.

The Alabama Law Enforcement Agency (ALEA), which is investigating the case, “cited the law she sponsored as the reason they are not releasing the footage,” the Peoples family’s attorney, Leroy Maxwell Jr., said in a statement. Givan “and her legislation have done enough harm to the justice for Jabari movement.”

Law enforcement agencies across the country have faced lawsuits calling for access to body-camera footage. Last month, a Colorado judge ordered a local police department to release an unedited body-camera video capturing a police shooting of an unarmed man, arguing the department violated state law in withholding the footage. And in California, a state appeals court upheld a ruling requiring the city of Roseville to release body-camera footage of a police-involved shooting, saying a pending criminal investigation was not reason enough to withhold body-camera footage.

As the deaths of Black Americans at the hands of police officers sparked global protests in recent years, dozens of states passed laws governing the use of body-worn cameras. Jurisdictions poured millions of dollars into equipping police officers with body cameras and adopting rules meant to ease the accessibility of footage retrieved from those devices.

But many of those body-camera laws have fallen short of their transparency goals. The exemptions they carve out for law enforcement officials, who often can withhold video if releasing it would jeopardize the police investigation by identifying a potential witness or suspect, enabled them to be less forthcoming, said Nancy La Vigne, dean of the Rutgers School of Criminal Justice in Newark.

Oklahoma, Indiana and Michigan all passed state laws between 2015 and 2017 that allow authorities to withhold or redact body-cam footage if its release would undermine or affect an ongoing investigation.

“In almost every state in the country, even when there’s rules for public access, police have an escape valve. They can always claim that it would jeopardize an investigation that’s in progress in some way,” La Vigne said. “You would think if anyone would be able to view the footage, it would be family members.”

In Alabama, law enforcement officers and agencies have considerable leeway to shield body-camera footage from the public. Givan says her 2023 law, Alabama Act 2023-507, was supposed to make it easier for families to review the recordings by creating a pathway to formally request to see the video. The measure requires law enforcement agencies to disclose body-camera footage to the subject of the recording or the subject’s “personal representative,” such as their parent, court-appointed guardian, spouse or attorney.

But the law also carves out a key exemption for officials wary of sharing body-camera footage with family members: “A custodial law enforcement agency may choose to not disclose the recording if the disclosure would affect an ongoing active law enforcement investigation or prosecution.”

In a July 1 statement, ALEA said it declined the Peoples family’s June 30 request to review the footage “in the interest of protecting the constitutional rights of everyone involved, as well as prioritizing a thorough law enforcement investigation of the recorded subject matter.”

Civil rights attorneys say Alabama law enforcement agencies are taking advantage of the exemption in the state law in an effort to delay or outright block families from viewing body-camera footage. They point to the death of 52-year-old Phillip Reeder, whose family waited nearly a year for officials to share the full recording of his fatal August 2024 encounter with Irondale police.

For the Peoples family, the wait has been nearly a month.

“Just show us what happened to our child, please,” Peoples’s father, William Peoples, said during a news conference this month.

Although Givan believes the Peoples family should have been able to view the footage by now, she said ALEA exercised “their right in the law not to release the tape.”

Givan began drafting House Bill 289 after 21-year-old Emantic “E.J.” Bradford Jr. was shot and killed by police at a mall in Hoover, Alabama, in 2018. Givan said the Bradford family’s fight to view the police footage compelled her to act.

The original goal, she said, was to require law enforcement agencies to release the footage to the public. However, her Republican colleagues refused to consider the bill, going as far as to block a quorum in committee to discuss it.

“We are in a supermajority White, Republican-dominated state, and there was no appetite to move the bill,” said Givan, who is Black.

The mood among legislators shifted in January 2023, when 29-year-old Tyre Nichols was beaten by Memphis police and officials decided to release the footage of the deadly confrontation to the public, days after showing it to Nichols’s family.

That spring, Givan worked with several law enforcement agencies — including the District Attorneys Association and the Alabama Association of Chiefs of Police — to narrow the scope of her bill. Instead of easing the public’s access to body-camera footage, the measure was tailored to focus on relatives of the subject of the video. In April 2023, she formally introduced the bill, which ultimately received bipartisan approval in both chambers of the state legislature.

Under Alabama Act 2023-507, signed into law in June 2023, law enforcement officials must “promptly” disclose the portion of the recording relevant to the individual’s request or inform the person that the agency declined to fulfill their request.

But some experts, such as civil rights attorney Griffin Sikes Jr., criticized the law as being so “vague” that it hasn’t had an appreciable effect on efforts to increase access to body-camera footage. For example, law enforcement agencies are required to “disclose only those portions of the recording that are relevant to the individual’s request,” according to the text of the law.

“Who gets to decide what’s relevant to the subject?” La Vigne said.

Civil rights attorneys and criminal justice experts who spoke to The Washington Post said investigators take several factors into consideration when weighing whether to disclose the body-camera footage, including whether the recording identifies children, an officer, potential witnesses or a suspect.

ALEA declined to comment outside of its July 1 statement.

Civil rights attorney Martin Weinberg said releasing body-camera footage that features an officer who may or may not have been cleared of wrongdoing could affect “their due process if they’re identified.”

Still, La Vigne said investigators could address the privacy concern by redacting the footage to conceal their identities. “That takes some time, but it’s not really a reason not to release it altogether,” she said.

Givan acknowledged how controversial her bill has become.

“Am I pleased with my bill? Absolutely. Is it perfect? Absolutely not,” Givan said. “But it wasn’t written to be perfect. It was written that we were going to come back the next year to try to tweak it.”

Givan has introduced legislation annually that would amend the 2023 state law by barring law enforcement agencies from withholding body-camera footage from families for more than six months. None has advanced.

In the meantime, Peoples’s relatives, local officials and community advocates hope protests will pressure ALEA to release the body-camera footage from the fatal police encounter. Eric Hall, co-founder of the Black Lives Matter chapter in Birmingham, Alabama, said taxpayers should be able to watch “the whole story and not just see pieces” of violent police encounters.

“We’re still begging for something that we pay for,” he said.
